title: Friendly Sharpness-Aware Minimization
main_claims: The batch-specific stochastic gradient noise component in SAM's adversarial perturbation is the primary driver of SAM's generalization improvement, not the full gradient component.
The full gradient component in SAM's perturbation actually degrades generalization by increasing dataset-level sharpness inconsistently with the per-minibatch minimization step.
F-SAM, which removes the full gradient component via an EMA approximation and retains only the stochastic noise component, outperforms vanilla SAM while being robust to perturbation radius choices.
methodology: SAM's minibatch gradient perturbation is decomposed into a full-gradient projection and a residual stochastic-noise component. Ablations (SAM-full, SAM-db, SAM-noise) isolate each component's effect on CIFAR-10/100 and fine-tuning tasks. F-SAM uses an exponential moving average of historical gradients to estimate the full gradient, then subtracts it from the minibatch gradient to obtain the noise-only perturbation. Convergence is proved for non-convex problems. Experiments use ResNet-18, VGG16-BN, and DeiT-S on CIFAR and Oxford datasets.
key_results: SAM-noise (using only the noise component) achieves 81.21% on ResNet-18/CIFAR-100, versus 80.88% for vanilla SAM and 78.02% for SAM-full.
F-SAM demonstrates superior generalization performance and better robustness to perturbation radius across multiple datasets compared to vanilla SAM.
As minibatch size for the perturbation step increases (strengthening the full-gradient component), SAM's classification accuracy on CIFAR-100 monotonically decreases.
limitations: Theoretical analysis assumes SGD as base optimizer; convergence guarantees for Adam-based variants are not provided.
EMA approximation of the full gradient introduces a hyper-parameter λ whose interaction with learning rate schedules is not fully characterized.
Experiments are limited to classification on standard CIFAR/ImageNet-subset benchmarks; no OOD corruption benchmarks (CIFAR-C) are tested.
relevance_to_rq: Directly relevant to the RQ's 'why SAM works' sub-question: F-SAM provides evidence that SAM's generalization gains come from stochastic noise in the perturbation rather than loss sharpness reduction per se, challenging a purely sharpness-centric explanation of SAM's OOD gains.
